findings.text: The total consent fee structure for CTE for a capital investment of Rs 10 crore is Rs 1,00,000 for a healthcare unit, which participants called unfavorable.

The application needs jamabandi, trace/type map, non-encumbrance certificate, revenue clearance certificate, and (for agricultural land) a non-agricultural land certificate from the Circle Officer; getting an up-to-date jamabandi and trace map from the Circle Office was described as a separate exercise of several weeks by itself.
A healthcare unit does not discharge industrial effluent, only bio-medical waste, but is charged on the same basis as industrial effluent.
The local authority (e.g. village panchayat) NOC has no fixed time; participants said this is the item most likely to hold up the whole file, with no way for the applicant to push it.
Queries come in installments rather than as one consolidated list of shortfalls; each objection means another visit, another document and another few weeks.

The fee is linked to capital investment (including land and building), not pollution load, so a low-emission unit on expensive Guwahati land pays more than a dirtier unit on cheaper land elsewhere in the state.
There is no deemed approval for CTE.
There is no settled practice of issuing one complete shortfall letter within a fixed number of days of receipt — queries are not consolidated.
Site inspection is not scheduled transparently: no advance notice to the applicant, no published calendar, and no facility to propose dates.
There is no pre-application guidance — no counter or facility where a first-time applicant can have the site and category checked before spending on documents and consultants.
The DPR is prepared separately for the bank, for the Industries department and for PCB Assam, in three formats, with the same underlying content.
Documents cleared at CTE stage are examined again at Consent to Operate stage without reference back to the CTE file.
Kamrup (Metro) has a dense concentration of units against limited technical staff at the regional office.
Query cycles restart the clock — the notified timeline can be met on paper while the applicant waits months in practice.
Show live status on the portal: current desk, days elapsed, days remaining against the notified timeline.
Auto-fetch land records from the state land records system instead of asking the applicant for a physical jamabandi and trace map.
Engaging a consultant is near-universal and is not seen as optional — a measure of how difficult the process is to navigate directly.

gaps.text: ED describes a single deficiency-query mechanism (20 days to respond, timeline restarts once from the date clarification is received). FGD participants instead describe queries arriving 'in installments' — objections come one after another, each requiring another visit, another document and another few weeks — a materially different experience of the query process than a single consolidated query.

ED's documented fee structure does not address sector-specific treatment for healthcare/biomedical-waste units; FGD participants say they are charged on the same consent-fee basis as industrial effluent dischargers despite discharging bio-medical waste, not industrial effluent.

ED's timeline breakdown does not give a time limit for the local-authority (panchayat/urban body) NOC sub-step; FGD participants say this item 'has no fixed time' and is the single item most likely to hold up the file, with no way to escalate it.
No FGD-specific good practice beyond what ED already documents (e.g. OCMMS upload discipline) was independently corroborated by this FGD session.

findings.text: Since March 2025, every CTO application must carry environmental monitoring reports (effluent, stack emission, air quality); units must pay for lab testing and wait for reports before they can even apply.
Information is spread over more than one place (Sewa Setu/EODB portal, the Board's own consent portal, and the Board website), so owners are not always sure where to apply and what to attach.
The stated time limits are long for Red category units (70 to 120 working days), making it difficult to plan a start or a renewal.
The monitoring-report condition applies to all categories of industry — a Green unit must meet the same condition as a more polluting unit.
CTO fee is fixed on total capital investment, not on how much a unit actually pollutes.

Under the November 2024 central notifications, some projects are exempt from Consent to Establish if they take an Environmental Clearance, but they still need CTO and the Board still raises the applicable CTE fee.
Application is online with an SMS/email acknowledgement, but the work is split between the Sewa Setu/EODB portal and the Board's own consent portal.

Instructions are not the same everywhere: some older Board pages describe fee payment by demand draft, while the Sewa Setu service page says online payment; participants said they do online payment only.
The unit has to arrange its own effluent, stack emission and ambient air reports before applying, adding extra cost.
The same documents (unit details, pollution control device details) are given again at Consent to Establish, initial CTO, and every renewal.
Monitoring reports are now needed with each CTO application, over and above the pollution-control-system details already given.
Units that needed Environmental Clearance must attach a copy of it again at the first CTO.
Time depends on category: 30 working days for Green, 40 for Orange, and 70 to 120 for Red, with the longest time for Red projects under the EIA guideline.
The application is complete only after monitoring reports are attached, so time is lost first in arranging lab testing.
A physical visit is often needed to hasten the process.
One portal and one checklist for CTO, listed category-wise (Green/Orange/Red), with the Board website and Sewa Setu showing the same instructions.
For Green and Orange units, keep monitoring reports simple and ask for them at fixed intervals instead of with every application.
Show application status and remaining days online, with SMS alerts at each stage.
Moving the process online is seen as a good step, but since it is still under development, and lack of awareness among users, delay still occurs.

quotes.speaker: Tirap Talukdar (Participant)
quotes.quote: They have introduced CCA (consolidated consent and authorisation) that comprises of all certificates covering waste (solid, municipal, biomedical) approval. But this has not been communicated to users. Not even on the portal. So it creates big confusion.

gaps.text: ED's CTO record does not mention a 'CCA' (Consolidated Consent and Authorisation) scheme covering solid/municipal/biomedical waste certificates; an FGD participant describes this as newly introduced but not communicated to users or shown on the portal.

ED describes the CTO process as online for submission, payment, tracking and download. FGD participants report that some of the Board's own older pages still describe fee payment by demand draft, while Sewa Setu's service page says online payment only — an inconsistency in the official information itself that the ED record does not flag for CTO (though it is flagged for FNO).

Neither the ED record nor this FGD session's timeline fully explains the November 2024 central-notification exemption from CTE for projects holding an Environmental Clearance, or why the Board reportedly still raises the CTE fee component for such projects when they apply for CTO.

ED's documents list for CTO does not state an effective date for the environmental-monitoring-report requirement; FGD participants date this requirement to March 2025 and describe it as applying uniformly across all pollution categories, which is not elaborated in the ED record.

findings.text: The seven-day promise does not match what happens: the clock starts only after a satisfactory inspection report, and the wait for the inspection itself ran from one to four months in cases participants described, with nothing in the published standard covering that period.

Nobody can tell the applicant how long the NOC stays valid; participants held certificates described variously as valid for one year, two years, or with no expiry written on them at all, and most learned the NOC had lapsed only when a GMC or factory inspector asked for it.

Files come back because the wrong form was used; the NOC is issued on separate forms by activity, and participants said they were told only weeks after submission that a different form applied, losing a month each time.
One office at Panbazar handles the whole state; participants travel to Guwahati headquarters repeatedly even for a routine query, with no counter in the industrial belt.

Rule 18(2) of the Assam Fire Service Rules, 1989 fixes seven working days from a satisfactory inspection report, but fixes no time limit for carrying out the inspection itself — the longest, least certain stage sits outside any service standard.
The validity period of the NOC is not prescribed in the rules or on the service page, even though a renewal form (Form XII) and a fourteen-day renewal timeline exist.
Choosing the right form is left entirely to the applicant, with no guidance note and no scrutiny at the counter; the error surfaces only after the file has sat for weeks.

Offline submission is the real route: the service is listed on Sewa Setu, but industrial applications do not run through to inspection online, so the paper file remains operative with no reliable tracking number.
Inspection observations differ from officer to officer on the same kind of premises (hydrant pressure, staircase width, extinguisher placement) — what one officer accepts, the next does not.
Shortfalls are communicated verbally at the site with no standard written deficiency memo, so the unit does not know precisely what to rectify and no re-inspection date is given.
The GMC-approved building plan, ownership/lease papers and identity proof are filed again with the fire application although GMC already holds the identical set.
The same drawings go in twice — once for the provisional NOC at plan stage, and again for the final NOC after construction.
Any change of trade, partner or internal layout voids the existing NOC under its own printed conditions and requires a fresh application with new drawings, however minor the change.

The inspection is the bottleneck: one office covers the whole state and visits are scheduled by officer availability, so the date depends on how hard the applicant follows up rather than when he applied.
Re-inspection restarts the clock, since the seven working days run from a satisfactory report — every round of observations resets the timeline to the beginning.
Fix a time limit in the Rules for the inspection itself (e.g. within fifteen days of a complete application) so the published standard covers the whole process, not only the last step.

Publish a form-selection guide and a threshold table (building height, floor area, Class A/B/C industrial definitions) and make scrutiny of the form compulsory at the counter before the file is accepted.
The NOC itself is free of cost, so the burden is time and consultancy rather than fee; participants reported paying roughly Rs 50,000 to Rs 2 lakh to consultants for an industrial fire NOC.
The clearance blocks others: without the fire NOC, the GMC occupancy certificate and the factory licence do not move, so a delay here compounds across departments.

quotes.speaker: Nalin Jain (Participant)
quotes.quote: Seven days, they say. Seven days after the inspection. The inspection took three months.

gaps.text: ED states the hazard-based validity date is 'printed as a valid-up-to date on the certificate'; FGD participants report holding certificates 'with no expiry written on them at all,' directly contradicting the ED's description that every certificate carries a printed validity date.

ED states a fee was introduced on the EoDB portal in 2024 for the Fire Safety Recommendation, NOC, temporary structures and Fire Attendance Certificate. FGD participants describe 'the NOC itself is free of cost,' with the only cost being consultancy and equipment — a direct contradiction on whether a statutory NOC fee currently applies (though ED's own remarks separately flag this cross-platform inconsistency).

ED's timeline text acknowledges cases 'of nearly 2 months' for the compliance-report-to-NOC stage; FGD participants describe the earlier inspection-wait stage alone (after the initial application, before any recommendation) commonly running one to four months — a longer, more specific range than the ED record states, suggesting real experienced delay may be understated.

ED does not quantify the real cost burden to applicants; FGD gives a concrete anecdotal range of roughly Rs 50,000 to Rs 2 lakh in consultant and equipment costs for an industrial fire NOC, which is useful data the ED record lacks.

findings.text: A weighbridge or fixed platform scale in a factory cannot be moved, so an officer has to come to the site; the site visit is hard to get scheduled and no visit date is given in advance.

For verification of a weighbridge, the unit has to arrange standard test weights and the vehicle to carry them; this arrangement, plus production stoppage during testing, costs more than the departmental fee, after which the weighbridge is left idle.
Several participants said that due to lack of awareness, they learned about registration as a packer of pre-packed commodities only when an officer visited, not at the time they started packing.
Inspections have no fixed time limit and are carried out on a regular, and sometimes surprise, basis.
There is no deemed approval provision for verification or for licence renewal, so a unit with a lapsed stamp has no legal cover until the process is completed.
A licence can be issued or renewed for one to five years, but participants said they generally renew every year, so the paperwork and the visit repeat annually.
Labelling requirements under the Packaged Commodities Rules overlap with FSSAI labelling — the same label gets examined by two different authorities against two different checklists.
Sewa Setu lists the service but redirects the applicant to the Assam EODB portal, which needs a separate registration and login, causing confusion about where to check status.
The date of the verification visit is not communicated on the portal or by SMS/email, so the unit has to keep someone free and follow up by phone.
There is no single point of contact for an application, and participants get different answers on status from different people at the office.
Trade licence, PAN and GST details are asked for again at every renewal, even though the department already holds them from the original licence.
The model approval certificate issued by the Government of India is asked for repeatedly, although it is a central document that does not change for the same model.
The same firm and premises details are submitted separately for the dealer licence and for the packer registration, as two unconnected applications.
The number of Legal Metrology officers covering Kamrup Metro is limited, and the load peaks in the renewal months.
Files move between the district office and the Controller's office, which adds time the applicant cannot see.
Send the scheduled verification visit date to the applicant by SMS within a few working days of the application, the same way the acknowledgement is sent.
Allow one consolidated application covering all instruments at one premises, so a single site visit clears everything instead of separate visits on separate dates.
Link the Sewa Setu and EODB logins so the applicant registers once and can track status in one place.
Actively offer the multi-year licence option of up to five years at renewal, so units are not repeating the same paperwork every year.

gaps.text: ED's LEM record does not discuss overlap between Legal Metrology labelling requirements under the Packaged Commodities Rules and FSSAI labelling checks; FGD participants raise this as a distinct duplicative-compliance burden not covered in the ED interview.

ED's process description (step 2) treats metrology.eodbassam.in and Sewa Setu as interchangeable access points. FGD participants instead describe Sewa Setu as redirecting them to a separate Assam EODB portal requiring its own registration and login, which they say causes real confusion — a more friction-laden picture than ED's process description suggests.

FGD participants suggest a single consolidated application covering all instruments at one premises with one site visit — an additional reform idea not among the ED's suggested reforms (which covered slot booking, third-party verification, longer re-verification cycles, and a composite multi-year fee).

Neither ED nor this FGD session gives a specific figure for how many Legal Metrology officers actually serve Kamrup Metro; FGD independently corroborates ED's capacity-constraint finding but adds no further quantification.

findings.text: Applicants apply online on the Sewa Setu portal, but still have to go to the Inspectorate office at Dispur again and again to follow up — online does not save the visit.
Applicants do not get proper status updates and cannot tell whether the file is with the Inspector, waiting for a reply, or simply pending.
Objections come one by one rather than all at once: the drawing is corrected and resubmitted, then a new objection comes, and each round adds more days of delay.
Approval is needed for installations above 650 volts, and the process is the same for a small unit and a big plant — a small MSME with a modest load faces the same paperwork as a large factory.
The service is nominally under the Assam Right to Public Services Act, but in practice nobody tells applicants the date by which they will get the approval.
There is no simple checklist or sample drawing format; different officials ask for different corrections, so the drawing cannot be prepared correctly the first time.
Even after online application, printed copies and signed letters are often asked for at the office.
There is no tracking of the file after submission, and no clear person to contact if it is stuck.
The building permission or approved plan from the local authority is asked for again at the drawing stage, even though the factory already has it from earlier approvals.
The same electrical layout and load details are submitted separately to APDCL for the power connection and to the Inspectorate for approval.
If load is added or the machine layout changed later, a fresh set of documents is asked for again.
The Inspectorate has few officers for the whole state, with several posts reported vacant; one officer covers many files and inspections.
Files move manually, and the Inspectorate and APDCL do not share information with each other, so applicants run between the two offices.
Because of the repeat visits, many units hire a consultant or contractor to follow the file, adding cost.
Electrical drawing approval, APDCL connection and local authority permissions should be on one window, with one application and one set of documents.
Show a fixed number of days on the portal with SMS/email at each stage, and give a sample drawing format and checklist.
Give all objections together in one go, not in rounds; simplify the process for small and low-risk loads.
For a new unit, the power connection and production cannot start until the drawing is approved — delay means machines lying idle while loan instalments and rent continue.
Going to Dispur from industrial areas in and around Guwahati costs a working day each time, plus transport cost.

quotes.speaker: Prasant Salkia (Participant)
quotes.quote: We submitted the building approval again for the drawing, though we had already given it earlier. Also, nobody tells us how many days it will take. We cannot plan our machine installation.

gaps.text: No official ED record exists for Electrical Drawings approval in Assam to cross-check this FGD-only record against; no notified processing-day figure is given by participants despite the service being nominally covered by the Assam Right to Public Services Act.
No specific fee figure is given by participants for this service; only indirect consultant/contractor costs from repeat visits are mentioned without being quantified.
No specific number of vacant Inspectorate posts or officer-to-file ratio is given; participants only describe the shortage qualitatively.

The Inspectorate (Power Department, lift/electrical matters) and APDCL do not share information, forcing applicants to run between two offices for what is functionally one underlying load/layout dataset.

findings.text: Renewal falls due every single year, with the full fee again and thirty days of processing, for a factory where nothing has changed; participants said the licence year now governs their calendar more than production does.

The dates do not work together: the department says apply at least fifteen days before the factory is taken into use, but allows itself thirty days to process the application — participants said it is simply not possible to comply with both, so a unit either starts late or starts unlicensed.
The penalty runs only one way: 25% extra is charged if renewal is not applied for thirty days before expiry, but nothing follows if the department itself takes longer than thirty days to issue.

Fees still go through a treasury challan under a particular head of account, with the original receipt to be produced, even though online payment through eGRAS exists; a wrong head or a photocopy sends the file back.

Two timelines apply and neither fits the third rule: the Citizen's Charter allows thirty days for registration and licensing, the Assam Factories (Amendment) Rules, 2017 prescribe forty-five, and neither is reconciled with the requirement to apply only fifteen days before the premises are used.

Assam provides auto-renewal for the Shops and Establishment licence and for contract labour licences, but not for the factory licence, although the factory has already been inspected and holds an approved plan and an accepted stability certificate.

An amendment of the licence is required merely to increase the number of workers or the installed horsepower — ordinary growth, such as taking on extra hands for a season, is treated as a regulatory event needing prior permission.
A duplicate licence requires an FIR receipted by the local police station — losing a paper certificate is treated as a police matter rather than an administrative one.

The file depends on documents the same office issued earlier (plan approval letter, accepted stability certificate), but these are not drawn from the department's own record and have to be filed again by the applicant.
Scrutiny is not consolidated: objections on the occupier nomination, the board resolution and the fee schedule came one after another rather than together.

Partnership deed, articles of association, memorandum, list of directors and the board resolution nominating the occupier are filed at plan approval and filed again at registration and licensing a few weeks later.
The same set goes in afresh at every transfer, every amendment and, for most units, at every annual renewal, even where none of it has changed.
Trade licence, land documents and identity proof already held by GMC are filed again here, and again with the fire and pollution authorities.
Annual renewals for every registered factory in the state are processed through one head office, producing a predictable backlog in the renewal months.
Vacant inspector posts shown in the department's own charter mean a file waits for an officer to be available rather than for a decision to be taken.
The licence cannot issue until the stability certificate has been accepted and the plan approval is on record, so a gap in either stops the licence file entirely.
Participants said informal payments are expected at renewal, when a unit has no choice but to get the licence before expiry; four of six described the renewal month as the point of greatest exposure.
Extend the licence term to three or five years with an annual self-declaration and risk-based inspection, removing most paperwork volume without reducing oversight.

Introduce auto-renewal for the factory licence on the same basis Assam already uses for Shops and Establishment and contract labour licences, on a declaration that premises, plan and machinery are unchanged.
The real cost is time: participants reported two to six weeks of staff effort every year on renewal alone, besides consultant charges of roughly Rs 20,000 to Rs 60,000.

findings.text: Two offices approve one building: GMDA issues the planning permit and GMC then issues the building permit. Participants did not know the planning permit was not the final permission; two had begun work on it and received notices.

The process is called online but still runs on paper: after online approval the applicant hands in four hard copies of the plans to GMDA, and three further sets travel from GMDA to GMC; every revision means reprinting all seven sets.

Nobody informs the applicant of anything: the bye-laws put the burden on the applicant to visit the counter within thirty days of submission to find out what is happening, with no call, letter or message when an objection is raised.

Timelines quoted differ wildly: the GMC page says the whole procedure usually takes forty-five days, officials have quoted thirty, and consultants advertise ten to fifteen, while participants reported three to nine months for an industrial or commercial building.

The master plan against which GMDA checks land use ran only to 2025 and has expired, with a revised plan still being prepared; zoning answers now turn on individual interpretation rather than a current notified plan.

Permission lapses and is deemed cancelled if construction does not begin within the validity period, but no corresponding time limit binds the authority to decide — the entire time risk rests on the applicant.
Nineteen separate documents are needed across the planning and building permit checklist, and neither authority publishes a single consolidated list, so the requirement is learnt in instalments.
The file passes from the Town Planner to the CEO at GMDA, then to the Associate Planner and the Commissioner at GMC; participants could see the file had moved but never what was holding it.

GMC attributes most delay to incorrect or faulty documents filed by the architect, while applicants say the requirement was never stated at the outset; there is no pre-scrutiny at the counter when the file is accepted.

Backlogs are cleared through special camps rather than routine processing; a GMC camp ran up to 31 December to clear pending building permissions and occupancy certificates, taken by participants as proof the normal channel does not work.
The same drawings and land documents go to GMDA and are then sent again to GMC — seven hard-copy sets in all, besides the online upload.
Land documents are examined separately by GMDA for the planning permit, by the Deputy Commissioner for land sale permission, and once more by GMC at the building permit stage.
For industrial buildings, the same drawings and land papers go again to the Chief Inspector of Factories for factory plan approval and to the Fire Service for the NOC, each in multiple copies.
Approval is sequential, not parallel: the GMC clock starts only when GMDA forwards the file, so any delay at the first stage pushes the second back with no overall limit.
Objections are raised one at a time and only on a visit, so each round of correction costs a fortnight or more before the next objection surfaces.
Participants said informal payments are expected at the scrutiny stage in both offices; four of the six described this as routine for commercial and industrial files.
Make it one application and one decision: GMDA and GMC should scrutinise the same drawings in parallel through a single window, with one permission and one overall statutory time limit.
Notify the revised master plan and publish one consolidated version of the bye-laws, withdrawing the superseded 2006 and 2014 texts.

Issue every objection in writing as a single consolidated list, with a reply date for the applicant and a decision date for the authority; complete the digital process, accept digitally signed drawings and end the seven-hard-copy requirement.

GMC collected only about Rs 2.5-3 crore against a target of Rs 16 crore from building permissions in 2024-25, read by participants less as a collection failure than as a sign of how many buildings go up without permission because the process is unworkable.

This approval is the gateway clearance: factory plan approval, the fire NOC, the water connection and the occupancy certificate all depend on it, so delay here holds up every other approval in the chain.

findings.text: The same building plan must be approved twice, once by the Chief Inspector of Factories and once by GMC; each office asks for a reference or NOC from the other, and participants described months of going back and forth between the two.

One office at Betkuchi approves plans for the entire state, and several inspector posts shown in the department's own charter are lying vacant; participants said their file was waiting for an officer to be available rather than for a decision.

Rule 3A requires simultaneous application to the Chief Inspector and to GMC/local body for the same building; two authorities approve the same drawings under different standards and neither is bound by the other's decision.

The plan application needs an NOC from the local authority while that authority's own plan approval runs in parallel; the order in which the two are to be taken is not settled anywhere, so the applicant is told after the fact that he chose wrongly.

No deviation of any kind from approved plans is allowed without fresh written permission — ordinary changes during construction (shifting a machine, moving a partition, adding a panel) require going back to the Chief Inspector.

No acknowledgement carrying a file number is given at the counter; follow-up is by telephone to a named officer or by travelling to the office, and the numbers listed on the department's charter no longer correspond to the person holding the post.

Objections on the drawings come one at a time instead of as a single list — participants were asked first about aisle width, then on the next visit about ventilation, then about the electrical panel position.

The same drawings, land documents and ownership/lease deed go separately to GMC and to the Chief Inspector of Factories, in multiple hard copies to each.

Hazardous units file fifteen sets of documents to the Site Appraisal Committee and then substantially the same material again with the plan application.
The land NOC, the fire NOC and the GMC approval all have to be in hand, and the factory file simply stops whenever any one of them is pending.
Vacant inspector and certifying surgeon posts shown in the department's own charter, combined with a single point of approval for the whole state, drive delay.

Participants said informal payments are expected to get drawings scrutinised and the file put up for signature; three of six said this decides whether a file takes two months or six.
Reconcile the three timelines through a single notification and state one enforceable period for plan approval, counted from a complete application.
Move Form No. 1 and the drawings online with a tracked application number and digital submission of plans.
Integrate factory plan approval with GMC building permission through the state single window, so one set of drawings and land documents serves both, and fix the NOC sequence in the rules.

findings.text: The original licence must be handed in with the renewal application, and the department then takes up to thirty days; for that whole period the factory runs with no licence document in hand, while GMC, fire and pollution inspectors continue to ask to see one.

Applying thirty days before expiry plus a thirty-day processing time means the renewed licence routinely arrives on or after the expiry date; participants carry a photocopy of the acknowledgement and hope it is accepted.
The fee is recalculated each year on the number of workers and installed horsepower, so the renewal is also an assessment; a dispute over the worker figure holds up the renewal itself.
The penalty is one-sided: 25% over the original fee is charged if the application is not received thirty days before expiry, but nothing follows if the department exceeds its own thirty days.

The protection that premises 'shall be held duly licensed' applies only where the application was filed in time, but nothing requires the department to issue any interim document evidencing that protection.

Assam already allows auto-renewal for Shops and Establishment, contract labour and interstate migrant workmen licences; the factory licence is excluded, although the premises, approved plan and accepted stability certificate are all on the department's own record.
The licence is annual with no risk differentiation; a low-risk unit with an unchanged plan and clean record renews on the same cycle, with the same paperwork, as any other factory.
No reminder is issued before expiry; tracking the thirty-day deadline is left entirely to the unit, and missing it by a single day costs 25%.

Where a unit has taken on more workers or added horsepower during the year, a separate amendment of licence is required, and the amendment and the renewal are not processed together even when filed together.
Documents like partnership deed, articles of association, list of directors and occupier nomination are filed again at renewal although the department already holds them from registration.
The original licence issued by the department has to be surrendered back to the department to obtain the next one.
The fee working on worker strength and horsepower is submitted afresh each year, although the department receives the same figures through annual and half-yearly returns.
Renewals for registered factories across the state are handled by one head office within the same season, so the queue is longest exactly when every unit needs its licence.
Vacant inspector posts shown in the department's own citizen's charter mean a renewal file waits for an officer to be free rather than for a decision.
Participants said informal payments are expected at renewal, because a unit cannot afford to be without a licence; four of six described renewal as the point of least bargaining room.

Make renewal automatic on a self-declaration that premises, plan, machinery and worker strength are unchanged, on the same basis Assam already applies to Shops and Establishment and contract labour licences.
Extend the licence term to three or five years, with fee payable annually if required, separating the paperwork cycle from the payment cycle.
Send an automatic reminder sixty and thirty days before expiry, and allow the fee to be paid fully online.
Participants reported two to six weeks of staff time each year on renewal, besides consultant charges of roughly Rs 20,000 to Rs 60,000, recurring every year regardless of any change in the factory.

findings.text: For most industrial locations a piped connection is simply not available — the Guwahati Jal Board is commissioning the network area by area, and an application can only be made once the unit's area appears on the list; unit owners in non-commissioned areas said the service does not exist for them yet.

Because piped supply is absent or undependable, almost every unit runs on its own borewell/tubewell, shifting the real regulatory burden to the groundwater NOC from the Central Ground Water Authority, which is a central process with no office in Assam to walk into.
There is no fixed time attached to the survey and estimate stage.
There is no published rate card for a non-domestic or bulk industrial connection.
The applicant has to arrange the right of way himself, and any road cutting needs a separate permission, handled entirely outside the water connection application.

(Session 2) Industrial applicants are told to come to the Executive Engineer's office with all required details, unlike household connections which go through the online portal; once filed, there is no way to know where the file is, requiring three to four visits just to check whether the feasibility inspection had been done.
(Session 2) The feasibility stage is where everything stops — waiting of two to five months for the engineer's site visit was common.
(Session 2) Even after the connection is released, supply is irregular because of shutdowns and pipe bursts, with water pressure too low or too high and irregular timing.
Water supply programmes for Guwahati are planned around household connections; industrial and bulk demand is not separately planned for, which is why units end up on groundwater by default.
There is no deemed approval provision for this service, even though it is notified under the Assam Right to Public Services Act.
The requirement of a digital flow meter and a hydrogeological report under CGWA guidelines pushes even small units towards hiring a consultant.

(Session 2) Connection is tied to the phased commissioning of the JICA-funded Guwahati water supply network; a unit in a non-commissioned zone has no route to a connection, and zone-wise status is not published. Two authorities (GMC Water Works Wing and the Jal Board, which charges a metered tariff) supply water under different rules, and participants were unclear which applies to them.
The application is online (Sewa Setu or the GJB mobile app), but everything after submission — survey, estimate, deposit, actual laying of the line — is offline and not visible on the portal.
The applicant is not told the site survey date in advance, so someone from the unit must be available without notice or follow up repeatedly; there is no single point of contact.

(Session 2) Documents already submitted are re-verified in original at the field feasibility visit; where that visit comes months later, applicants are asked to bring a fresh set, and the document list requested varies by official (e.g. trade licence/GST asked by some, not others).

(Session 2) The service line usually needs road cutting, requiring separate permission and restoration charges from GMC or PWD with no joint process, so the applicant runs between offices while the water file waits.

Land documents, holding number and the GMC property tax receipt are asked for again even though the same records sit with GMC; in session 2, the GMC property tax receipt is reportedly demanded up to three times (application, feasibility visit, and fee payment).
The water requirement and water balance details prepared for the CGWA NOC are asked for again by the Pollution Control Board in a different format.
(Session 2) A change of firm name, partner or ownership requires the entire document set to be filed again as a fresh application, with no short amendment route for a connection already sanctioned.
The 21 working-day timeline is counted from a complete application, but in practice the survey and estimate stage sits outside any timeline and is where most of the waiting happens.
Applications from areas not yet commissioned under the ongoing water supply project stay pending until the area is ready, with no indication of when that will be.
(Session 2) Feasibility inspection depends on a single engineer for the zone; inspections are clubbed and carried out only once enough applications collect in one area.

(Session 2) Files move physically between the section clerk, Assistant Engineer, Executive Engineer and accounts branch with no register or receipt the applicant can see; rejections on technical grounds (wrong pipe size, missing signature) come late, after months, restarting the process.
Publish a rate card for non-domestic and bulk connections, so a unit knows the likely deposit and monthly charge before applying.

Show the survey date and the estimate on the portal, with an SMS to the applicant, the same way the application acknowledgement is sent; (session 2) give SMS updates and visible file status exactly as already done for household connections.
Have one application point that routes the file to GMC, the Jal Board or PHED based on location, so the unit does not have to work out which agency it falls under.

(Session 2) Fix a timeline in the Regulations for each stage (acknowledgement, feasibility inspection, sanction, release) and make a written, reasoned order compulsory for every rejection or query, so a refusal can be questioned.

(Session 2) Bring road cutting permission and restoration into a single window with the Jal Board, and publish zone-wise commissioning status; accept AIIDC/GMDA allotment letters, registered lease deeds and trade licence as valid proof of property where a GMC tax receipt does not exist.

Participants said the practical choice for an industrial unit in Guwahati today is a borewell, not a piped connection, so the real cost of regulation for this service is mostly the cost of the groundwater NOC and its compliance conditions.
(Session 2) Participants compared the process unfavourably with the electricity connection from APDCL, which they said at least gives an acknowledgement and a date to work against.
